newsitem.title: USA: American, pilots recess talks to avert strike.
newsitem.headline: American, pilots recess talks to avert strike.

text.p: Negotiations between American Airlines and its pilot union recessed late on Tuesday night without an agreement to avert a strike set against the number two U.S. air carrier.
Talks will resume on Wednesday, and a federal mediator said he remained hopeful the two sides would reach a settlement before the deadline of midnight on Friday.
"I would characterize the talks thus far as a frank discussion of the issues and exploration of options," Kenneth Hipp, chairman of the National Mediation Board, told reporters.
Hipp said earlier that mediators "remain hopeful" of an early settlement that would avert the walkout threatened by the Allied Pilots Association if no new contract was reached.
Shutting down American would disrupt the travel plans of some 200,000 passengers on the 2,200 routes the carrier flies each day worldwide.
In shuttle negotiations on Tuesday, the two sides met separately and then with mediators trying to broker an accord between management and the pilots.
Hipp declined comment when asked if progress had been made, saying mediators would not discuss "where we are in terms of the issues and how we are progressing."
But union president James Sovich said a request by the company for clarification of items it thought were already resolved were "counter-productive."
He also said in a report to the 9,000 pilots the APA represents that American had yet to respond to a new contract settlement proposal the union submitted a month ago.
Sovich added, however, that the union's board of directors would be in Washington Wednedsay if needed to act on any contract offers. The board had been set to arive from Dallas Thursday.
There was no immediate comment from American on whether the company thought progress had been made in the talks.
The APA is seeking a 11.5 percent pay raise and stock options over a four-year contract. American, a unit of Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., has offered 5 percent.
Also at issue is American's plan to add jets to its regional carrier American Eagle and use lower-paid pilots in another union to fly them. The APA wants its members to fly those planes.

The issue is over jurisdiction and outsourcing, with the APA now flying all of American's jets and the lower-paid American Eagle pilots, represented by the Air Line Pilots Association, flying Eagle's smaller turboprops.

But American has argued that most of the other big national carriers have commuter lines that fly smaller jets, and it needs them, too, with lower-paid pilots in the cockpit, to remain competitive with its national rivals.

American has said a strike would force the unpaid furlough of most of its 90,000 American and American Eagle workers, and cost the company up to $50 million a day. It says it has arranged bank loans of up to $2 billion to help it through any strike.
The hardest hit cities would likely be American's home base of Dallas-Forth Worth and its hubs in Chicago, Miami, New York, Los Angeles and San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Federal mediators stepped into the talks after union members rejected a tentative agreement in January and later negotiations failed to bridge the management-union gap.

American says its pilots are among the highest paid in the industry and that new demands would cripple its ability to compete, threatening its growth and a $6.5 billion order for up to 103 jetliners from Boeing Co..
But union leaders are quick to point to the company's announcement last month that it ran up record profits of $1.02 billion last year.

The Senate aviation subcommitee has urged President Clinton to help mediate the dispute, but the White House said it would not act unless asked by both sides, although it was closely monitoring the negotiations.
